title: row03
live_proof: measured 2026-10-16 as well as inspected. fts5MultiIterNew stores a raw Fts5Structure* in Fts5Iter.pStruct; a write under an active cursor releases that structure, and the re-seek's teardown releases it again. Host ASan: heap-use-after-free, 0 bytes inside a freed 40-byte region -- offset 0 is Fts5Structure.nRef, the struct's first member -- read in fts5StructureRelease (sqlite3.c:195026) <- fts5MultiIterFree <- sqlite3Fts5IterClose <- fts5ExprNearInitAll <- fts5ExprNodeFirst <- sqlite3Fts5ExprFirst <- fts5CursorReseek <- fts5NextMethod. fts5StructureRelease is 'if( pStruct && 0>=(--pStruct->nRef) )', so the stale operation is a read and a decrement, and a second free if the result reaches zero. Fixed upstream in 3.27.0, which deletes the cached field outright
object: the Fts5Structure the multi-iterator cached a raw pointer to
lifetime_ender: a table write under the live cursor releases the structure, after which the iterator's own teardown releases it again

note: Re-measured 2026-10-16; every verdict holds and one explanation is corrected. The case's own header said nRef at offset 0 is the granule memsys5's 8-byte Mem5Link overwrites, so in the domain the refcount read returns a freelist integer rather than faulting. That is not what happens. Probe site 50 marks the caching store in fts5MultiIterNew, every release with the nRef value it reads, and the free: across 31 release hits on native memsys5, on virtual Capstone with lookaside off and on CheriBSD purecap, the address judgement reports witnesses=0 -- the block is never free when it is read -- and the event trace for the busiest structure shows why: CACHE, four releases down to nRef=1, FREE, then the SAME address is CACHEd again with a fresh nRef=3. memsys5 reissues the block to the next Fts5Structure, which is the same size class, before the stale release arrives. So the stale --nRef does not read allocator bookkeeping; it silently decrements the refcount of a LIVE successor object. The Mem5Link would only be visible if the block were still free at the read, which it never is here. That makes the case a better illustration of why identity matters than the header claimed: the memory is not garbage to be sanity-checked, it is another object's valid data, so no value-based or address-based oracle can see the access, and Sublet's cause-25 is the only arm that rejects it. fts5's own integrity-check returns rc=0 afterwards on CheriBSD, so the corruption is not visible to the engine either
